discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: A series of systems will bring widespread precipitation, gusty winds, and increase the potential for coastal flooding along with high surf throughout much of the upcoming week. A weak upper ridge may produce somewhat quieter weather over the upcoming weekend, but overall unsettled conditions are expected to persist.
hydrology: Wetter systems moving into the region through this week will start to bring some rises to area rivers. At this time, no widespread river flooding is expected, however the Skokomish River will likely reach flood stage around midweek and topping into moderate, possibly near major given latest guidance. A river flood watch has been issued for Mason County from Wednesday morning through Sunday afternoon.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A series of systems will bring widespread precipitation, gusty winds, and increase the potential for coastal flooding along with high surf throughout much of the upcoming week. A weak upper ridge may produce somewhat quieter weather over the upcoming weekend, but overall unsettled conditions are expected to persist.

sections.title: Short term (today through Thursday)
paragraphs: No major forecast updates have been made this morning. See below for previous forecast discussion with an updated aviation and marine section.

The first of a series of frontal systems is spreading precipitation inland across Western Washington early this morning. A series of frontal waves will slow its eastward progression. As a result, we'll likely see a lull in precipitation, especially across the interior, later this morning into the afternoon. What is left of the front will eventually drag onshore this evening for another uptick in precipitation. Winds will remain gusty through the period, particularly along the coast, where a wind advisory is in effect.

Any relative lull in precipitation (and wind) on Wednesday will be brief at best as a 160 knot jet streak west of 140W drives a more vigorous frontal system toward the region. Impacts associated with this system will likely be more widely felt. Though the parent low with this system stays well to our northwest, it will produce a strong southeasterly gradient capable of producing high wind Wednesday night into early Thursday along the coast as well as across the North Interior. Precipitation with this system will also be more significant with totals between 00Z Thursday and 00Z Friday of 2+ inches along the coast, 3 to 5 inches in the Olympics, 1.5 to 3 inches in the Cascades, and around an inch for the interior lowlands outside of the Olympic rain shadow. Snow levels will be well above the passes through the period.

In addition to periods of widespread precipitation and gusty winds, coastal flooding and high surf will also be of concern. High surf and low atmospheric pressure coinciding with some of the highest tides of the year will create the potential of major coastal flooding. Conditions will likely peak on Wednesday along the Pacific coast and Thanksgiving Day for inland coastlines.

sections.title: Long term (Thursday night through Monday)
paragraphs: A fair degree of uncertainty hangs over the early portion of the extended forecast. A number of ensemble members build an upper ridge into California toward the weekend, but Western Washington is simply too far north to really benefit from that as systems ride over the top of the ridge into the area. Once again, and stop me if you've heard this before, any break will be brief. Ensembles show good agreement by early next week with another broad upper trough taking up residence offshore for a return to more active conditions as December arrives.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Breezy easterly to southeasterly gusts have been occurring this morning with a front stalled offshore. This front will move inland tonight, keeping the forecast for breezier conditions across area terminals valid through today. Cigs remain VFR across the area with rain showers continuing throughout the day, lowering overnight to MVFR. Another, stronger front will arrive Wednesday night into Thursday for more widespread rainfall and gusty winds. The highest gusts (35-45kt) will be along the immediate coast and northern terminals. Other locations will generally see gusts between 25-35 kts through Thursday.

KSEA...VFR cigs persist with gusty easterly to southeasterly winds. There have also been reports of LLWS with the winds that will be peaking later this morning into early afternoon. Rain will be in and out of the terminal through the day as the front slowly begins moving onshore. Wind gusts will increase again Wednesday night into Thursday to 25-35 kts as the next frontal system arrives. Rain will be heavy at times as that system moves through.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Low pressure will remain offshore through the majority of the week, with a couple of fronts remaining remaining stalled offshore. The headlines remain in place through Tuesday evening - storm force wind gusts in the outer coastal waters, with gale gusts continuing in the inner coastal waters, and the west/east Strait of Juan de Fuca. Winds will slowly decrease through the day into tonight/first part of Wednesday, but will still remain gusty with gale force wind gusts in the coastal waters and east Strait of Juan de Fuca. Gale warning headlines were extended in these areas through Wednesday afternoon, except for the west strait which has the gale warning replaced with a small craft advisory (SCA) this afternoon into Wednesday. SCA's will also continue for the northern inland waters and Admiralty Inlet into Wednesday afternoon, and the central strait through early Wednesday morning as winds decrease below any headline thresholds.

Thursday's fronts remains on track to bring another round of potentially strong winds to the coastal waters (up to storm force). Gale force winds are also likely to continue in the east strait, and are also possible in the northern inland waters Thursday. As winds shift more to the southwest remaining waters will likely see winds strong enough to impact small craft. Friday will see a reprieve from the strong winds of this week, with winds not picking back up until later in the weekend (only affecting small craft in the coastal waters and west portions of the strait).

Seas will build up to 18 to 22 ft with long periods today into Wednesday (there is also an SCA for the Grays Harbor bar where rough to severe bar conditions will occur with the combination of strong ebbs and high seas). The seas will hold at 18 to 22 ft through Friday where they will decrease to 10 to 13 ft, and 6 to 8 ft Saturday before building back to 10 to 13 ft early next week.
HPR

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: An active weather pattern is expected through this week with repeated relatively warm systems bringing rain to the region, a first today into Wednesday morning and a second, more potent atmospheric river Wednesday night through Thanksgiving Day. Coastal and marine weather hazards remain the primary concern this week as strong winds offshore and rough seas coincide with monthly King Tides, raising the chances for coastal flooding.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: An active weather pattern is expected through this week with repeated relatively warm systems bringing rain to the region, a first today into Wednesday morning and a second, more potent atmospheric river Wednesday night through Thanksgiving Day. Coastal and marine weather hazards remain the primary concern this week as strong winds offshore and rough seas coincide with monthly King Tides, raising the chances for coastal flooding.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Monday...A broad area of low pressure remains located over the Northeast Pacific while an associated cold frontal boundary over 100 miles offshore as of early Tuesday morning. This boundary will slowly move eastward toward the coast, ultimately pushing inland from this afternoon into this evening as the parent low steadily weakens off of Vancouver Island. The majority of rainfall will be focused along the north Oregon and south Washington coasts, before heights rapidly rise aloft on Wednesday in the wake of the weakening front, leading to a drying trend through the day although rain shower are most likely to linger through Wednesday along the coast and in southwestern Washington. Through Wednesday afternoon, there are 60-90% chances of 0.5 inches of more of rainfall accumulating in the Coast Range/Willapa Hills and to the west, 10-25% through interior southwestern Washington, and 10% or less in interior northwestern Oregon including Portland.

While the front remains offshore, an offshore-oriented pressure gradient (-6 to -8 mb between Portland and the Dalles) will continue to support gusty east to southeast winds across the region. The strongest winds are expected along the coast as the front moves onshore this afternoon and evening as southeast winds shift out of the south with gusts up to 30-40 mph. Inland, areas of favored gap easterly flow will also see stronger gusts, especially at the western entrance to the Columbia River Gorge where higher terrain and exposed ridgetops may see peak gusts up to 70 mph. Elsewhere across the eastern Portland metro, peak gusts of 30-45 mph are more likely, decreasing farther away from the Gorge.

Another area of low pressure over the Northeast Pacific will bring the next period of active weather from late Wednesday through Thanksgiving Day. There is good consensus that a strong atmospheric river with peak IVT of 750-1000 kg/ms will traverse the region, resulting in significant rainfall accumulations. Minimizing the flood threat, however, will be the relatively shorter duration of heavy rainfall and a sub-optimal orientation for forcing peak rates of orographic ascent. Nonetheless, median 48-hour rainfall amounts from Wednesday afternoon through Friday afternoon are 1.25-2 inches along the I-5 corridor and 2-3 inches along the coast and in areas of terrain. In the reasonable worst case (10% chance of occurrence), locales along the coast and in terrain may see up to 4 inches while the I-5 corridor may see as much as 2-3 inches. In the case of these higher end amounts, flooding concerns remain largely limited to nuisance flooding of typical low-lying, urban, or other poor drainage areas. As is typical with warm ARs, snow levels will rise well above the Cascade passes, mitigating any winter travel concerns.

As the AR moves onshore, south-southwest winds over the nearshore waters may support a coastal jet, resulting in along-shore accelerations and higher winds out of the south at beaches and headlands. Chances for peak gusts of 60 mph or higher on Thursday remains 25-50% along much of the coast, highest in Tillamook, Clatsop, and Pacific Counties. Chances for impactful southerly wind gusts of 45 mph or higher within inland valleys are 10-15% or less.

Forecast uncertainty increases into this weekend; the majority of long-range ensemble members continue to favor upper-level ridging and relatively drier conditions over the West Coast Friday into Saturday, but 30-40% of members maintain chances for rain through this period. Chances for further upper-level troughing and associated rain increase again Sunday into early next week. -36

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 18z Wednesday...Headed through the rest of the day and tonight, VFR conditions likely persist across the region thanks in-part to easterly flow keeping CIGs elevated. A front stalled offshore will see light rain showers stream across the region from southwest to northeast as the day progresses with increasing coverage as the boundary finally moves onshore through this afternoon and evening. As the lower levels begin to saturate during this time period, cigs lower to 4-7 kft by 21-24z with the highest chances (10-30%) for MVFR cigs at coastal terminals this afternoon and tonight.

Near the Columbia River Gorge at KPDX and KTTD, east winds continue to gust around 30-35 kt before easing after the front moves onshore and gradients weaken late this afternoon and tonight. Within the Willamette Valley, winds instead remain below ~10 kt, increasing slightly out of the south near the frontal passage. Just ahead of the front, low-level wind shear remains a concern. Winds aloft at Portland-area terminals are likely to remain light enough to avoid wind shear mentions in TAFs, but 2-kft winds of 40-50 kt out of the south atop east to southeast winds at 10-15 kt at coastal terminals do merit LLWS inclusion into the afternoon, especially at KAST.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...VFR conditions are expected through the TAF period. East-southeast winds will continue to gust to 25-35 kt before steadily easing as the approaching front moves onshore and weakens the pressure gradient around 23z-06z. Directional wind shear looks to peak in the 2-3 kft layer and is therefore not included in the TAF. Dry east winds maintain elevated cigs ahead of the front, with low (10-15%) chances for MVFR cigs as the bulk of frontal rain arrives this afternoon and evening. Conditions trend drier for Wednesday morning. -99/36

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Continued active weather will maintain hazardous marine conditions through much of the workweek. A frontal system stalled offshore will continue to support elevated chances for storm-force gusts through today, especially beyond 30-40 NM. Storm Warnings therefore remain in effect over the waters beyond 10 NM through 4 PM this afternoon before conditions begin to ease behind the front. Gale Warnings otherwise remain in effect across the inner waters including the Columbia River Bar through tonight, as well as across the outer waters beginning this evening. A robust southwest swell will build to 15-20 ft at 12-14 seconds through tonight while southerly wind-driven seas also near 15 ft. These combined will yield significant wave heights of 19-23 ft, peaking this afternoon.

Behind the frontal passage and in the relatively brief lull between weather systems, a west-southwesterly swell will move into the waters on Wednesday, supporting Hazardous Seas Warnings for seas of 15-20 ft across the waters on Wednesday. Another, more potent system arriving late Wednesday into Thanksgiving Day will bring another round of potentially hazardous winds and seas. At this point, gale conditions are most likely across the waters, however at least isolated storm- force winds cannot be ruled out. As confidence increases in the timing of this next system, additional Gale or Storm Watches are likely to be issued for Wednesday evening and Thursday.
A return to calmer marine conditions is favored from late in the workweek into the weekend. -36

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: A Coastal Flood Advisory remains in effect through the middle of the week as the combination of King Tides, elevated seas, and the arrival a longer period swell likely leads to tidal overflow - impacts are most likely at high tide. Coastal residents in the warned area should be alert for rising water, and take appropriate action to protect life and property. It's also worth highlighting the moderate to high sneaker wave threat today through Wednesday and Thursday. Beachgoers should exercise caution, stay far back from incoming waves, and remain observant of the ocean. Avoid logs, large rocks, and jetties.
